content: There are well-established methods for implementing changes and creating systems to sustain those changes once a specific goal has been achieved. Quality improvement is a management approach that healthcare professionals can utilize to reorganize care delivery, ensuring that patients receive high-quality healthcare. Quality improvement is defined as systematic and continuous actions that lead to measurable improvements in healthcare services and the health status of targeted patient groups. The process of quality improvement has been extensively studied, and there are well-developed models for its application in healthcare. These include frameworks developed by the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia, the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI), and the US Department of Health and Human Services. Quality improvement processes are cyclical and consist of the following steps: (i) planning a change in the quality of care, (ii) implementing the changes, (iii) measuring the changes in care practices and/or outcomes, and (iv) analyzing the changed situation to either further improve or maintain the practices. In the IHI model, these steps are referred to as Plan, Do, Study, and Act (PDSA), and they are often visualized as a cycle. In the context of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI), the PDSA cycle can be applied to improve the implementation of each of the Ten Steps. This methodology is particularly important for steps that facilities find challenging or for which global standards have not yet been achieved. Once the desired level of performance is reached, the implementing team can focus on monitoring the performance of sentinel indicators. The quality improvement approach is highly relevant to the BFHI, and countries are strongly encouraged to adopt this approach. It enhances sustainability by requiring fewer external resources or additional staff due to the establishment of standard processes. Regardless of the quality improvement model used, several key principles are central to its success: The triad of planning, improvement, and control is fundamental. Implementing teams need clear guidance on how to navigate these steps. Active participation of frontline service providers, such as nurses and physicians, is essential. These individuals are best positioned to identify what works and the obstacles they face in practice. Leadership engagement is critical. Facility administrators, department heads, and thought leaders must be convinced of the importance of breastfeeding protection, promotion, and support. They should encourage frontline implementers to adapt their practices as needed and actively support necessary changes. Measurement and analysis of progress over time are vital. Using data to identify problem areas allows for a more focused approach to addressing them. Teams should decide on key indicators to measure, in addition to sentinel indicators. External evaluation or assessment is important. Quality assurance systems implemented by national or decentralized authorities can validate results and ensure adherence to agreed standards. Indicators from relevant appendices can be used for external assessments. The visualization of the four steps of quality improvement—Plan, Do, Study, Act—illustrates the iterative nature of the process. In the revised BFHI, this approach is integral to achieving universal coverage and sustaining the program over time. At the national level, leadership and coordination are critical to ensuring that all mothers and newborns receive timely, evidence-based care tailored to their needs. Transforming the quality of services to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding in all facilities requires a health-systems approach. The WHO Health Systems Framework outlines six core components, or building blocks, relevant to BFHI implementation: service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, financing, and leadership/governance. The primary objectives of a national BFHI program should be to achieve 100% coverage and sustain recommended practices over time. Countries are called upon to implement nine key responsibilities of a national BFHI program, which include establishing a national breastfeeding coordination body, integrating the Ten Steps into national policies and standards, ensuring the competency of healthcare professionals, utilizing external assessment systems, developing incentives for compliance, providing technical assistance, monitoring implementation, advocating for the BFHI, and securing sufficient resources for ongoing funding. National leadership and coordination are essential for achieving high coverage and sustainability. Integration into national policies, improving healthcare professional training, external assessment processes, incentivizing change, and providing technical assistance are particularly important for achieving universal coverage. National monitoring, continuous communication, advocacy, and secure financing are critical for long-term sustainability. Each of these responsibilities is interconnected and explained in greater detail throughout the guidance. For example, the establishment of a national breastfeeding coordination body is vital. This body should be multisectoral, including representatives from government, academia, professional organizations, NGOs, and community-based organizations. It should exclude actors with conflicts of interest, such as companies producing infant formula or feeding bottles, to maintain the integrity and credibility of the BFHI. Policies and professional standards of care must integrate the Ten Steps into relevant national policy documents and professional standards. Governments can mandate adherence to these standards through legislation, regulation, accreditation, or certification. For instance, legislation can require facilities to have a breastfeeding policy and prohibit the acceptance of donations of breast-milk substitutes. Facility accreditation can depend on adherence to clinical standards and management procedures. Healthcare professionals must have adequate knowledge, competence, and skills to implement globally recommended practices for breastfeeding protection, promotion, and support. Facilities are responsible for assessing competencies and ensuring that all staff have the necessary knowledge and skills. Pre-service training for all relevant professions should include adequate time and attention to breastfeeding, including theoretical and practical sessions. Where pre-service training is inadequate, new competency-based national curricula may need to be developed.
